So now that we have a baseline to go off, how big of a moon rock would we need to reach an equivalent to the tungsten (19250 kg/m^3) rod? Well we need at least a mass of 9 metric tons. From the lunar samples collected, the moon consists primary of basalt (3270-3460 kg/m^3), feldspar (2840-2910 kg/m^3), and breccia a composite material (3030-3050 kg/m^3). Let's be generous and assume the densest material is mined, 3460 kg/m^3. That means, to be a 9 ton equivalent mass, a hunk of moon rock approximately 2.6 m^3. So a sedan sized object would have to be lobbed at the Earth assuming 100% mass retention on atmosphere entry, which is unlikely, so some additional mass would be needed. How much mass? The ultimate question is, how much mass of lunar rock would you need to reach an equivalent energy yield of "100s of times" that of a 25 Mt nuclear device. Well the energy equivalent of a 1 ton of TNT is 4.184x10^9 Joules of energy, so a 25 Gigaton nuclear device would be 1000 Petajoules of energy (or one quadrillionth the hourly energy production of the sun). From the equations of motion, we know that the kinetic energy of an object with mass moving at some speed is:

KE = .5 x mass x velocity^2

So assuming our mass driver, fires the rock at Mach 10 (3403 m/s), then we would need an object with a mass of 1.727x10^11 kilograms or a cube 368 m or 1100 ft on all sides. Now, assuming that there is no loss in the system, then the energy required to move that mass (the work) is equal to the kinetic energy, meaning that our moon base would have to produce 1000 Petajoules of electrical energy to put into the mass driver to throw this hunk of rock. To put that into perspective, that would be something like 1/30000th the total energy production of Earth in a year to shoot one rock of the requisite mass.

While the post in general is good, you made a couple of bad assumptions, chiefly that the "moon installation" (i.e. whatever you use to launch the hunk of rock) would have to impart all the kinetic energy to the rock in question.

The idea here is to get a rock out of the moon's gravity well and let it fall towards earth's gravity well. So you don't need the Mach 10 assumption (just the moon's escape velocity) and the final total energy would have to be calculated from the velocity of the rock at the time of impact (probably difficult unless some assumptions are placed on air resistance and such).

I assumed that the rock in question is a rough sphere 100 [m] in diameter, a drag coefficient of 0.5 (somewhat high, but it does not matter much), a linearly varying density for the atmosphere with a cutoff point located 100 [km] above sea level, took your data for density of the rock and such and dropping of said rock from the L1 Lagrange point of the Earth-Moon system. You can see the (very rough) code here PasteBin (you'll need Matlab or Octave to run it).

Here you can see a plot of position vs time of our rock as it's dropped, since L1 is an unstable equilibrium point you can see the derivative at the beginning it's almost 0 (it's actually 1e-6 [m/s], the intial velocity towards earth I gave it).

To get to L1 from the moon you need the energy necessary to achieve escape velocity on the moon (~2.28 [km/s]), this is El=0.5MrVl^2, for my 3500 [kg/m3] r=100 [m] rock this is ~3.81x10^16 [J] (a lot, but we could hurl smaller stones)

The gist of it is, assuming the rock does not break up in the atmosphere, it would impact the ground with a velocity of ~10715 [m/s], with an impact energy of 8.42x10^17 [m/s], this is ~22 times more energy that was required for launch and ~10000 times the energy of "Little Boy"

As you reduce the size of the rock, the final impact velocity gets reduced, for instance, a rock 10 [m] in diameter would hit at aprox. 8 [km/s], yielding ~4.69x10^14 [J] at impact (5 times little boy) and would "only" take 3.81x10^13 [J] to launch from the moon, so we are talking Terajoules instead of Petajoules.

All said and done, I'd say it's physically possible, but extremely unlikely in our lifetimes :)
